Exigent

/EK-sih-juhnt/ - the stress falls on EK · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Exigent means urgent, critical.

A dead phone battery is inconvenient; a snapped tow rope halfway up the cliff is exigent.

Worked Example

When the dam gauge passed its red line at midnight, the county's routines stopped mattering — the one exigent job was clearing the low valley, and every crew, van, and school bus was pulled onto it before dawn.

Exigent is stronger than 'important' and more specific than 'urgent' — an exigent situation demands action now, from whoever is nearest, and shoves everything else off the table until it is handled.

How Exigent Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

urgent

urgent: needs prompt attention; exigent turns the dial further — action this instant, whatever it costs

pressing

pressing: crowds to the front of the to-do list; exigent clears the list entirely

Antonyms

minor

minor: small enough to shrug off without consequences

optional

optional: safe to skip altogether

How Strong Is It? — pressing → urgent → exigent

pressing vs. exigent

pressing vs. exigent: Pressing stops short of exigent — a pressing task crowds the top of your list but can still wait for morning.

urgent vs. exigent

urgent vs. exigent: Urgent stops short of exigent — urgent means soon, while exigent means now, with people already moving.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ex-

Prefix — ex-: out

Root — ig

Root — ig: to drive, to do (a form of Latin agere)

Suffix — -ent

Suffix — -ent: in a state of

Put it together

Put it together: Ex- ('out') + ig- (a form of agere, 'to drive') + -ent = driving out, demanding. Latin exigere meant to drive out or to demand — an exigent situation is one that demands: it drives everything else out of the room until it gets an answer.

Use the root in a new word: agent

Use the root in a new word: agent: A travel agent does the doing for you — booking, changing, and rebooking the flights.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / technical

Exigent belongs to formal writing — legal opinions ('exigent circumstances'), incident reports, editorials. In conversation say urgent. Reach for exigent when you need urgency with institutional weight: a demand so immediate that normal rules and schedules give way to it.
